docs.title: Streamdaq v2
docs.text: Data quality monitoring for unbounded streams. Made easyier.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install streamdaq

Annotate

You can verify installation with pip show streamdaq. You can download a specific version with pip install --update streamdaq==<your_desired_version>.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
streamdaq allows you to monitor the quality of your data streams in just a few lines of Python code. Before we dive into the details, here is a complete example. Easy, isn't it? (1)

  1. This is an example annotation in plain text.
# pip install streamdaq
import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.checks import InRange, WindowDataQualityCheck
from streamdaq.measures import Count, DistinctCount, MostFrequent
from streamdaq.sessions import Session
from streamdaq.tasks import Task


def is_seven_frequent(most_frequent: tuple) -> bool:
    return 7 in most_frequent


# Step 2: Create a monitoring task that reads the stream and prints the results
task = Task(
    name="interactions",
    input=read_stream,  # (2)!
    output=output_sink,  # (1)!
    windowby_column="timestamp",
    include_window_bounds=True,  # (3)!
)

# Step 3: Define what Data Quality means for you
# Per-row checks, evaluated on every incoming element
task.add_instant_checks(
    InRange(name="valid_events", column="interaction_events", low=0, high=10),
)
# Per-window checks, evaluated on every tumbling window of 10 time units
task.add_window_checks(
    WindowDataQualityCheck("interaction_count", Count("interaction_events"), "(5, 15]"),
    WindowDataQualityCheck("my_freq", MostFrequent("interaction_events"), is_seven_frequent),
    WindowDataQualityCheck("interaction_distinct", DistinctCount("interaction_events"), "<= 5"),
    window=pw.temporal.tumbling(duration=10),
)

# Step 4: Kick-off monitoring and let Stream DaQ do the work while you focus on the important
Session(tasks=[task]).start()
  1. output accepts any function that takes a table. Here, every result row is printed as it arrives. Built-in sinks write to CSV, JSON Lines, Kafka, MQTT or Postgres instead.
  2. Any function that returns a Pathway table can be the input, for example one reading from Kafka, MQTT or a CSV file.
  3. Adds window_start and window_end as the first columns of every per-window result.
  4. Any output sink that emits a pw.Table
Output

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Understanding these concepts helps you design data quality monitoring that works in real streaming systems.

Why concepts matter

Stream processing has constraints that do not exist in batch workflows. These pages focus on the reusable ideas behind stream-first quality monitoring.

  • Stream-first Data Quality

    Why traditional data quality dimensions need adaptation for unbounded streams.

    Read more

  • Real-time Monitoring

    Late arrivals, watermarks, and practical latency/completeness trade-offs.

    Read more

  • Compact vs Native Data Formats

    Trade-offs between representation styles and when each one fits best.

    Read more

docs.title: Compact vs Native Data Formats
docs.text: In streaming systems (especially IoT and edge scenarios), two representation styles are common: native and compact formats.

docs.title: Native format
docs.text:
Native format stores each measurement as its own record.

Native format
{"timestamp": 1640995200, "sensor_id": "env_001", "field": "temperature", "value": 23.5}
{"timestamp": 1640995200, "sensor_id": "env_001", "field": "humidity", "value": 65.2}
{"timestamp": 1640995200, "sensor_id": "env_001", "field": "pressure", "value": 1013.25}

Strengths

  • Direct field-level access
  • Broad compatibility with existing tools
  • Flexible schema evolution

Costs

  • Repeated metadata in each message
  • Higher bandwidth and storage overhead

docs.title: Compact format
docs.text:
Compact format groups related measurements in one record.

Compact format
{
  "timestamp": 1640995200,
  "sensor_id": "env_001",
  "fields": ["temperature", "humidity", "pressure"],
  "values": [23.5, 65.2, 1013.25]
}

Strengths

  • Better transmission efficiency
  • Lower metadata redundancy
  • Better fit for constrained links/devices

Costs

  • Additional unpacking/transformation effort
  • More rigid producer/consumer schema coupling

docs.title: Choosing a format
docs.text:
Scenario Better fit Rich tooling, easy debugging, dynamic schemas Native Bandwidth-constrained IoT, high-frequency telemetry Compact

IoT reality

Compact formats are common in IoT because battery, bandwidth, and connectivity constraints reward smaller payloads.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Choose the format that fits your infrastructure and operational constraints. Monitoring design should still preserve clear semantics for time, identity, and field meaning.

docs.title: Stream-first Data Quality
docs.text: Data quality has been a cornerstone of data management for decades, but streaming data introduces constraints that traditional quality frameworks were not designed to handle.

docs.title: Traditional Data Quality Dimensions
docs.text:
Core dimensions used across data quality literature include:

  • Accuracy: Data correctly represents real-world entities and relationships.
  • Completeness: Required data is present without missing values.
  • Consistency: Data follows rules and constraints across records and fields.
  • Validity: Data conforms to expected formats, types, and ranges.
  • Uniqueness: Unwanted duplicates are absent.
  • Timeliness: Data is available when needed and reflects current state.

docs.title: The Implementation Gap
docs.text:
Research on open-source data quality tooling shows that conceptual dimensions and concrete implementations are often loosely coupled: different tools may implement the same dimension differently, and one check may support multiple dimensions.

Research insight

This mismatch creates a many-to-many relationship between theory and implementation, making quality definitions harder to compare across tools and projects. (1)

  1. Learn more in our publicly available research work, Unfolding Data Quality Dimensions In Practice

docs.title: Streaming Data Adds New Requirements
docs.text: When data is continuous and unbounded, quality definitions expand beyond static dataset checks.

docs.title: Completeness becomes temporal
docs.text: In streams, completeness is not only about nulls/missing fields, but also about expected arrival rates and sequence continuity.

docs.title: Accuracy without a full gold standard
docs.text: For unbounded streams, a complete reference dataset is rarely practical. Accuracy often relies on statistical expectations, cross-source consistency, and domain constraints.

docs.title: Timeliness is continuous
docs.text: Timeliness becomes an always-on property that must be observed over time, including late arrivals and delivery delays.

docs.title: Stream-native quality dimensions
docs.text:
Beyond traditional dimensions, stream settings emphasize:

Dimension Stream interpretation Velocity Data arrives at expected rates Ordering Events appear in an acceptable sequence Latency Processing or arrival delays stay in bounds Continuity Unexpected temporal gaps are absent

docs.title: Practical takeaway
docs.text: High-quality stream monitoring combines traditional data quality principles with time-aware, rate-aware, and sequence-aware checks.

docs.title: Real-time Monitoring
docs.text: Real-time data quality monitoring introduces challenges that do not appear in batch execution. The key is managing trade-offs explicitly.

docs.title: Key challenges
docs.text:
• Late arrivals: Events may arrive out of order due to network or processing delays.
  • Event time vs processing time: Systems process data at one time while the event occurred at another.
  • Watermarks: A strategy is required for deciding when to finalize results despite possible late data.
  • Backpressure: Input may exceed current processing throughput.

docs.title: Stream DaQ approach
docs.text:
Stream DaQ windows the stream by event time: you choose the column that holds when each event happened (windowby_column) and the window to group events by.

Event-time windows
task = Task(
    input=input_source,
    output=output_sink,
    windowby_column="event_timestamp",
)
task.add_window_checks(
    WindowDataQualityCheck("count", Count("value"), "(5, 15]"),
    window=pw.temporal.tumbling(duration=30),
)

Each window produces its results exactly once, as soon as the event time in the stream passes the end of the window. Records that arrive after that, for a window that has already been closed, are not counted in it.

To tolerate late records, keep each window open a little longer with wait_for_late, in the units of the time column:

Waiting for late records
task = Task(
    input=input_source,
    output=output_sink,
    windowby_column="event_timestamp",
    wait_for_late=5,  # report [0, 30) once event time reaches 35
)

Records for a window that arrive within the wait are still counted; later ones are left out.

docs.title: Latency vs completeness
docs.text:
• Without wait_for_late, window results are emitted as soon as each window closes, so latency stays low, but records that arrive too late for their window are left out, and out-of-order streams can under-count.
  • A larger wait_for_late counts more late records, at the cost of reporting every window later.

docs.title: Memory vs statistical stability
docs.text:
• Larger windows often improve statistical signal but need more memory.
  • Smaller windows reduce memory but can produce noisier metrics.

docs.title: Recommended starting point
docs.text:
1. Use the column that records when each event happened as windowby_column, not the arrival time.
  2. Measure your real arrival-delay distribution, and set wait_for_late to cover most of it.
  3. Tune window sizes to your data frequency and operational SLAs.
  4. Validate behavior under realistic traffic patterns.

# pip install streamdaq
import multiprocessing

import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.checks import InRange, WindowDataQualityCheck
from streamdaq.measures import Count, DistinctCount, MostFrequent
from streamdaq.sessions import Session
from streamdaq.tasks import Task


def main():
    # Step 1: Point Stream DaQ to your data stream (here, a tiny in-memory stream)
    def read_stream() -> pw.Table:
        return pw.debug.table_from_markdown(
            """
            user_id | timestamp | interaction_events
            UserA   | 1         | 7
            UserA   | 2         | 3
            UserB   | 3         | 7
            UserA   | 4         | 12
            UserB   | 5         | 5
            UserB   | 6         | 7
            UserA   | 7         | 9
            UserB   | 8         | 7
            UserA   | 11        | 2
            UserB   | 12        | 4
            UserA   | 13        | 4
            UserB   | 14        | 1
            """
        )

    def is_seven_frequent(most_frequent: tuple) -> bool:
        return 7 in most_frequent

    def print_to_terminal(table: pw.Table) -> None:
        pw.io.subscribe(table, on_change=lambda key, row, time, is_addition: print(row))

    # Step 2: Create a monitoring task that reads the stream and prints the results
    task = Task(
        name="interactions",
        input=read_stream,
        output=print_to_terminal,
        windowby_column="timestamp",
        include_window_bounds=True,
    )

    # Step 3: Define what Data Quality means for you
    # Per-row checks, evaluated on every incoming element
    task.add_instant_checks(
        InRange(name="valid_events", column="interaction_events", low=0, high=10),
    )
    # Per-window checks, evaluated on every tumbling window of 10 time units
    task.add_window_checks(
        WindowDataQualityCheck("interaction_count", Count("interaction_events"), "(5, 15]"),
        WindowDataQualityCheck("my_freq", MostFrequent("interaction_events"), is_seven_frequent),
        WindowDataQualityCheck("interaction_distinct", DistinctCount("interaction_events"), "<= 5"),
        window=pw.temporal.tumbling(duration=10),
    )

    # Step 4: Kick-off monitoring and let Stream DaQ do the work while you focus on the important
    Session(tasks=[task]).start()

    # Only needed in Jupyter notebooks: wait for the monitoring to finish, so its results
    # appear in the notebook. A plain Python script waits for it automatically on exit.
    for process in multiprocessing.active_children():
        process.join()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
This guide walks through everything Stream DaQ can do today, from defining a single check to running many monitoring tasks behind a REST API.

How Stream DaQ is organised

A task reads a stream, applies checks to it, and writes the results to an output. A session runs one or more tasks, each in its own process. You can build tasks in Python, or send them as JSON to the REST API.

flowchart LR
    S[Input source] --> I
    S --> W
    subgraph T[Task]
        I[Instant checks]
        W[Window checks]
    end
    I -->|per-row results| O1[Output]
    W -->|per-window results| O2["Output (_window)"]

  • Tasks and Sessions

    Define what to monitor, and run it.

    Read more

  • Instant Checks

    Check every incoming row: ranges, sets, patterns, comparisons.

    Read more

  • Window Checks

    Check groups of rows over time: windows, grouping, late data.

    Read more

docs.title: Advanced Examples
docs.text: Complete examples that combine several features.

docs.title: Grouping by several columns
docs.text:
groupby_column takes a single column. To check each combination of several columns separately, for example each unit of each plant, add a column that combines them, and group by that column.

This task checks every plant and unit separately, in 1-minute windows, waiting 5 seconds for late readings:

PythonREST API (EVB data) 
import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.checks import WindowDataQualityCheck
from streamdaq.measures import Count, Mean, StandardDeviation
from streamdaq.sessions import Session
from streamdaq.tasks import Task


class Reading(pw.Schema):
    timestamp: int  # epoch milliseconds
    plant: str
    unit_id: str
    temperature: float


def _group_key(*values: str | None) -> tuple[str | None, ...]:
    return tuple(values)


def read_stream() -> pw.Table:
    readings = pw.io.jsonlines.read("readings.jsonl", schema=Reading, mode="streaming")
    # One column combining the plant and the unit, e.g. ("P001", "012332")
    group = pw.apply_with_type(_group_key, tuple[str | None, ...], readings.plant, readings.unit_id)
    return readings.with_columns(group=group)


task = Task(
    name="per_plant_and_unit",
    input=read_stream,
    output=pw.io.jsonlines.write,
    output_kwargs={"filename": "quality.jsonl"},
    windowby_column="timestamp",
    groupby_column="group",
    wait_for_late=5_000,
)
task.add_window_checks(
    WindowDataQualityCheck("reading_count", Count("temperature")),
    WindowDataQualityCheck("enough_readings", Count("temperature"), ">= 6"),
    WindowDataQualityCheck("mean_temperature", Mean("temperature", precision=1)),
    WindowDataQualityCheck("stable_temperature", StandardDeviation("temperature"), "<= 2"),
    window=pw.temporal.tumbling(duration=60_000),
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    Session(tasks=[task]).start()

Over the REST API, the combined column is added by a custom source. This one reads EVB data from MQTT and combines the tags listed in group_by_tags:

evb_group_by_tags.py
import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.custom import source
from streamdaq.io.utils import ensure_unique_mqtt_client_id
from streamdaq.schema.evb.definitions import EVBSchema


def _group_key(*tag_values: str | None) -> tuple[str | None, ...]:
    return tuple(tag_values)


@source(name="mqtt_evb_grouped", data_format="compact")
def mqtt_evb_grouped(uri: str, topic: str, group_by_tags: list[str]):
    uri = ensure_unique_mqtt_client_id(uri)
    raw_table = pw.io.mqtt.read(uri=uri, topic=topic, format="json", schema=EVBSchema)

    def post_transform(native_table: pw.Table) -> pw.Table:
        # Tags can be missing from a message, so their columns may hold None
        tag_columns = [native_table[tag] for tag in group_by_tags]
        group = pw.apply_with_type(_group_key, tuple[str | None, ...], *tag_columns)
        return native_table.with_columns(group=group)

    return raw_table, post_transform

Start the server with it loaded, streamdaq serve --files evb_group_by_tags.py, and send:

[{
  "name": "per_plant_and_unit",
  "input": {
    "type": "mqtt_evb_grouped",
    "params": {
      "connector_params": {
        "uri": "mqtt://127.0.0.1:1883",
        "topic": "evb/data",
        "group_by_tags": ["plant", "unit_id"]
      }
    }
  },
  "output": {"type": "jsonlines", "params": {"filename": "quality.jsonl"}},
  "wait_for_late": 5000,
  "window_checks_config": {
    "windowby_column": "time",
    "groupby_column": "group",
    "window": {"type": "tumbling", "params": {"duration": 60000}},
    "checks": [
      {"name": "reading_count", "measure": {"type": "Count", "params": {"column": "time"}}},
      {"name": "enough_readings", "measure": {"type": "Count", "params": {"column": "time"}}, "must_be": ">= 6"}
    ]
  }
}]

Each window result names its group, so you can tell the plants and units apart:

{"window_start": 0, "window_end": 60000, "group": ["P001", "012332"], "reading_count": 12, "enough_readings": true, ...}
{"window_start": 0, "window_end": 60000, "group": ["P001", "012385"], "reading_count": 4, "enough_readings": false, ...}

A value missing from a row, such as an EVB message without a unit_id tag, shows as null in the group, and forms a group of its own.

docs.title: Assessments
docs.text:
An assessment decides whether a value is good. It's given as must_be, which is applied in both window checks and instant checks. The result column then holds True or False.

must_be can be written in four ways.

docs.title: Comparisons
docs.text:
An operator followed by a number:

must_be True when the value is ">= 5" at least 5 "> 5" more than 5 "<= 5" at most 5 "< 5" less than 5 "== 5" exactly 5

Spaces are optional (">=5" works too), and decimals are allowed ("<= 0.25").

Note

There's no "not equal" operator. Use a function (below) for value != 5.

docs.title: Ranges
docs.text:
Two numbers in brackets. A square bracket includes the bound, a round bracket excludes it:

must_be True when the value is "[1, 5]" between 1 and 5, both included "(1, 5)" between 1 and 5, both excluded "[1, 5)" at least 1 and less than 5 "(5, 15]" more than 5 and at most 15

The lower bound must be smaller than the upper bound.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Any function that takes the value and returns True or False:

def is_seven_frequent(most_frequent: tuple) -> bool:
    return 7 in most_frequent


WindowDataQualityCheck("seven_is_common", MostFrequent("events"), is_seven_frequent)

Functions are useful for values that aren't single numbers, such as the tuple from MostFrequent or the dictionary from Percentiles.

docs.title: Registered assessments
docs.text:
An assessment registered with @assessment can be used by its name. This is how custom assessments are used from the REST API, where functions can't be sent:

from streamdaq.custom import assessment


@assessment(name="IsWithinTolerance")
def is_within_tolerance(value: float) -> bool:
    return abs(value) <= 5


WindowDataQualityCheck("drop_ok", MaxDelta("temperature", time_column="timestamp"), "IsWithinTolerance")

See Custom Code. If a name is both registered and looks like a comparison or range, the registered assessment wins.

docs.title: Checking several conditions
docs.text:
A check has one must_be. To test several conditions on the same measure, add one check per condition:

WindowDataQualityCheck("not_too_few", Count("temperature"), ">= 5"),
WindowDataQualityCheck("not_too_many", Count("temperature"), "<= 100"),

or combine them in one range ("[5, 100]") or function.

docs.title: Compact Data
docs.text: Stream DaQ can monitor compact IoT messages in the EVB (Event Bus) format, where one message carries several measurements at once. Stream DaQ unpacks them into ordinary rows and columns, so all checks work on them as usual. See Compact vs Native Data Formats for the background.

docs.title: The EVB format
From messages to rows
docs.text:
Each reading in values becomes one row. The message above becomes:

time temperature humidity plant unit_id name type validation_errors_report 1645334535000 60 55 StreamdaqFactory 012332 TemperatureHumidity Points null 1645338135000 62 54 StreamdaqFactory 012332 TemperatureHumidity Points null
  • Fields become columns, and each tag becomes a text column.
  • validation_errors_report is null for a valid message. For an invalid one, it describes what's wrong, and the row is still kept, so you can check for it.

A message is invalid if, for example, its first field isn't time, a reading has a different number of values than there are fields, or a time doesn't have 13 digits.

Fields are matched by position

Values are assigned to columns by their position, using the field order discovered from the first message. Producers must always send the fields in the same order.

docs.title: Schema discovery
docs.text:
You don't need to describe the columns of compact data: Stream DaQ discovers them from the first valid message it receives. It waits up to 20 seconds; if no valid message arrives by then, the task fails with a timeout error.

The discovered columns are fixed from then on. Fields or tags that only appear in later messages don't become columns.

docs.title: Monitoring EVB data
docs.text:
Set data_type to "compact" in the source's settings, and use time as the time column. Durations are in milliseconds:

POST /api/v1/bulk_create
[{
  "name": "evb_quality",
  "input": {
    "type": "mqtt",
    "params": {
      "data_type": "compact",
      "connector_params": {"uri": "mqtt://127.0.0.1:1883", "topic": "evb/data"}
    }
  },
  "output": {"type": "jsonlines", "params": {"filename": "evb_quality.jsonl"}},
  "window_checks_config": {
    "windowby_column": "time",
    "groupby_column": "unit_id",
    "window": {"type": "tumbling", "params": {"duration": 5000}},
    "checks": [
      {"name": "enough_readings", "measure": {"type": "Count", "params": {"column": "time"}}, "must_be": ">= 1"}
    ]
  }
}]

The sources that support compact data are mqtt, kafka and python_connector, plus custom sources declared with data_format="compact".

docs.title: Grouping by tags
docs.text: Tags become ordinary columns, so you can check each unit separately with "groupby_column": "unit_id". To group by several tags, for example each unit of each plant, see Advanced Examples.

docs.title: Test data
docs.text:
EVBMockStream generates EVB messages for testing, including some deliberately invalid ones. Use it through the python_connector source:

"input": {
  "type": "python_connector",
  "params": {
    "data_type": "compact",
    "module": "streamdaq.schema.evb.mock_generator",
    "class_name": "EVBMockStream",
    "connector_params": {"nof_messages": 100, "sleep_between_sec": 0.1}
  }
}
Setting Default nof_messages 10 nof_non_time_fields 15 sleep_between_sec 0.0 values_min, values_max 0.0, 100.0 round_values 2

docs.title: Custom Code
docs.text: When the built-in pieces aren't enough, you can add your own measures, assessments, sources and sinks with decorators from streamdaq.custom. Once registered, they can be used by name, including from the REST API.

docs.title: Measures
docs.text:
@measure turns a function into a measure for window checks. The function receives the window's values, one sequence per column, and returns the measured value:

from typing import Any

from streamdaq.custom import measure


@measure(columns=["time", "measurement", "status"], name="MaxDropBetweenOkReadings", sort_by_column="time")
def max_drop_between_ok_readings(data: dict[str, Any]) -> float:
    """Largest drop in `measurement` between consecutive OK readings."""
    ok_values = [m for m, s in zip(data["measurement"], data["status"]) if s == "OK"]
    drops = [previous - current for previous, current in zip(ok_values, ok_values[1:])]
    return max(drops) if drops else 0.0
Setting Meaning columns The columns the function needs. data has one entry per column. name The measure's name; defaults to the function's name. Used in API payloads. sort_by_column If set, all columns are sorted together by this column, e.g. time. desc Sort in descending order (default False).

@measure turns the function into a measure class. Create it without arguments:

WindowDataQualityCheck("max_drop", max_drop_between_ok_readings(), "<= 5")

In an API payload, use its name with empty params: "measure": {"type": "MaxDropBetweenOkReadings", "params": {}}.

docs.title: Assessments
docs.text:
@assessment registers a function as a named assessment:

from streamdaq.custom import assessment


@assessment(name="IsWithinTolerance")
def is_within_tolerance(value: float) -> bool:
    return abs(value) <= 5 or value > 100

Use it with must_be="IsWithinTolerance", in Python or in an API payload.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
@source registers a function that creates the input table. Its keyword arguments come from the payload's connector_params.

Native dataCompact (EVB) data

The function returns a pw.Table:

import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.custom import source


class Reading(pw.Schema):
    timestamp: int
    temperature: float


@source(name="readings_from_kafka")
def readings_from_kafka(bootstrap_servers: str, topic: str):
    return pw.io.kafka.read(
        rdkafka_settings={"bootstrap.servers": bootstrap_servers, "group.id": "streamdaq"},
        topic=topic,
        format="json",
        schema=Reading,
    )

With data_format="compact", the function returns the raw EVB table and a function that Stream DaQ applies after converting the data to rows and columns:

import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.custom import source
from streamdaq.io.utils import ensure_unique_mqtt_client_id
from streamdaq.schema.evb.definitions import EVBSchema


@source(name="my_evb_source", data_format="compact")
def my_evb_source(uri: str, topic: str):
    raw_table = pw.io.mqtt.read(
        uri=ensure_unique_mqtt_client_id(uri), topic=topic, format="json", schema=EVBSchema
    )

    def post_transform(native_table: pw.Table) -> pw.Table:
        return native_table.with_columns(source="my_evb_source")

    return raw_table, post_transform

The schema is discovered from the first message, which calls your function once more.

Using a custom source in a payload
"input": {"type": "readings_from_kafka", "params": {"connector_params": {"bootstrap_servers": "localhost:9092", "topic": "readings"}}}

docs.title: Sinks
docs.text:
@sink registers a function that writes a result table. It receives the table and the payload's output params:

import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.custom import sink


@sink(name="jsonlines_with_source")
def jsonlines_with_source(table: pw.Table, **params) -> None:
    pw.io.jsonlines.write(table.with_columns(source="streamdaq"), **params)

Per-window results are passed to the sink with _window added to filename, topic_name, topic or table_name, if one of them is in the params. See Where results go.

docs.title: Loading custom code
docs.text:
Custom code has to be loaded before tasks use it, and in every task process:

  • With the server: streamdaq serve --files my_code.py. --files can be a file or a folder; for a folder, every .py file in it is loaded (not subfolders), except files whose names start with _.
  • In Python: import your module before creating tasks, and give the same path to the session, so the task processes load it too: Session(tasks=[...], files_path="my_code.py").

GET /api/v1/config/options lists everything registered, so you can check that your code was loaded.

A complete example with all four decorators is in examples/custom-code/my_streamdaq.py.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text: Practical notes that don't belong to a single feature.

docs.title: Jupyter notebooks
docs.text:
Each task runs in its own process, and session.start() returns while the tasks keep running. In a notebook, the cell can therefore finish before any results are printed.

To wait for the tasks to finish, join their processes after starting the session:

import multiprocessing

session = Session(tasks=[task]).start()

# Only needed in Jupyter notebooks: wait for the tasks, so their results appear in the notebook
for process in multiprocessing.active_children():
    process.join()

active_children() returns every child process started from the notebook, so this also waits for any other child processes running in the same kernel.

Tasks reading a stream that never ends keep running until they are stopped. To stop them, call:

session.gracefully_kill(timeout_seconds=5)

docs.title: Hot-swapping and Persistence
docs.text: Tasks created through the REST API are stored: they survive server restarts, and can be changed while running without starting over.

docs.title: Changing a running task
docs.text:
Send the task again to POST /api/v1/bulk_create, with the same name and the new configuration. Stream DaQ then:

  1. starts a new version of the task with the new configuration;
  2. stops the old version, about a second later;
  3. continues from where the old version stopped, using the task's watermarks.

The response says "<name> was hot-swapped". Each change increases the task's version, which appears in every result row:

{"_streamdaq_metadata": {"task_name": "readings", "task_version": 2}, ...}

Note

For about a second, both versions run at the same time and can both write results. Use task_version to tell their rows apart.

docs.title: Restarts
docs.text:
When streamdaq serve starts, it resumes every task that was running when the server stopped, from its watermarks. Tasks that had finished are kept in the store but not restarted. Use --clear to start from an empty store.

A task that can't be rebuilt, for example because its custom code wasn't loaded with --files, is skipped with a warning, and the other tasks still start.

docs.title: Watermarks
docs.text:
A task's watermarks record how far it got:

  • Instant watermark: the latest event time processed by the instant checks. When the task resumes, rows from that time onwards are processed.
  • Window watermark: the end of the latest window reported. When the task resumes, windows start from that point.

docs.title: What is stored where
docs.text:
Everything is stored under the server's --root folder:

Path Contents .streamdaq_db/ Task configurations and versions. .internals/watermarks/<task name>/ Each task's watermarks.
  • Deleting a task (DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{name}) removes its configuration and watermarks.
  • --clear removes both folders.

docs.title: In Python
docs.text:
In Python, a task's input and output are plain functions, so you can use any of Pathway's connectors directly:

import pathway as pw


class Reading(pw.Schema):
    timestamp: int
    unit_id: str
    temperature: float


def read_stream() -> pw.Table:
    return pw.io.kafka.read(
        rdkafka_settings={"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092", "group.id": "streamdaq"},
        topic="readings",
        format="json",
        schema=Reading,
    )


task = Task(
    name="readings",
    input=read_stream,
    output=pw.io.kafka.write,
    output_kwargs={"rdkafka_settings": {"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092"}, "topic_name": "quality"},
    windowby_column="timestamp",
)
  • Input: any function returning a pw.Table. It's called as input(**input_kwargs).
  • Output: any function taking a pw.Table, called as output(table, **output_kwargs). Window results go to a destination with _window added, see Where results go.

docs.title: In the REST API
docs.text:
Tasks sent to the REST API pick a source and a sink by name, with their settings in params:

"input": {
  "type": "jsonlines",
  "params": {"path": "readings.jsonl", "schema": {"timestamp": "int", "unit_id": "str", "temperature": "float"}}
},
"output": {"type": "jsonlines", "params": {"filename": "quality.jsonl"}}

GET /api/v1/config/options lists every source and sink available, including custom ones.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
type Reads Compact data jsonlines JSON Lines files, with Pathway's pw.io.jsonlines.read no mqtt An MQTT topic, with pw.io.mqtt.read yes kafka A Kafka topic, with pw.io.kafka.read yes python_connector A Pathway Python connector class from an importable module yes parquet A Parquet file, read once (not streamed) no csv CSV files, with pw.io.csv.read no

Settings shared by all sources:

Setting Meaning data_type "native" (default): one value per column. "compact": compact messages, several measurements per message. schema The columns and their types, e.g. {"timestamp": "int", "unit_id": "str"}. Types: "int", "float", "str", "bool", "bytes". Required for native JSON data. mode jsonlines and csv only: "streaming" (default, keeps watching for new data) or "static" (reads once). connector_params Settings passed to the Pathway reader as they are. If left out, every other setting (apart from those above) is passed instead.

Source-specific settings:

  • mqtt: uri (e.g. "mqtt://127.0.0.1:1883") and topic. A unique client_id is added to the URI automatically, so several tasks can read the same broker.
  • kafka: rdkafka_settings and topic, as in Pathway.
  • python_connector: module and class_name of a pw.io.python.ConnectorSubject; other settings are passed to the class.
  • parquet: path.

Known limitations

  • csv: the schema setting isn't passed to Pathway, which requires one, so CSV tasks fail when they start. Use jsonlines, or a custom source, until this is fixed.
  • kafka: the source currently adds a group.id setting that Pathway rejects, so Kafka tasks fail when they start. A custom source calling pw.io.kafka.read works in the meantime.
  • Compact data with schema: with data_type: "compact", leave schema out and let Stream DaQ discover it. Giving a schema currently fails.

docs.title: Sinks
docs.text:
type Writes with Typical settings jsonlines pw.io.jsonlines.write filename csv pw.io.csv.write filename kafka pw.io.kafka.write rdkafka_settings, topic_name, format mqtt pw.io.mqtt.write uri, topic (a unique client_id is added automatically) postgres pw.io.postgres.write postgres_settings, table_name

A sink's params are passed to the Pathway writer as they are, so see Pathway's documentation for every option.

Columns named time or diff

Pathway's writers add their own time and diff fields to every row. If your input has a column with one of these names, which every EVB stream does, the per-row results clash with them: Kafka and MQTT refuse to write, and JSON Lines keeps only Pathway's value. Per-window results aren't affected.

docs.title: Where results go
docs.text:
A task writes up to two result streams to its output: per-row results from instant checks, and per-window results from window checks. Per-row results go to the destination given in the output settings. Per-window results go to the same destination with _window added to the first of these settings found:

Setting Per-row results Per-window results filename quality.jsonl quality_window.jsonl topic_name (Kafka) quality quality_window topic (MQTT) quality quality_window table_name (Postgres) quality quality_window

If none of them is present, both result streams go to the same destination. This applies to custom sinks too.

docs.title: What the output rows look like
docs.text:
Every row written by a sink contains the result columns, plus two fields added by Pathway:

Field Meaning diff 1 for a new row, -1 when an earlier row is withdrawn (e.g. replaced by an update). time Pathway's processing time for the row: when it was produced, not when the event happened.

Window results are reported once per window, so they're always diff: 1.

docs.title: Instant Checks
docs.text:
Instant checks are applied to every row as it arrives. Each check adds one True/False column, named after the check, to the per-row results, next to all the input columns.

from streamdaq.checks import InRange, InSet, Regex

task.add_instant_checks(
    InRange(name="valid_temperature", column="temperature", low=-30, high=50),
    InSet(name="known_unit", column="unit_id", allowed_values={"012332", "012385"}),
    Regex(name="valid_plant_code", column="plant", regex=r"P\d{3}"),
)
One per-row result
{"timestamp": 1645334535000, "temperature": 21.5, "unit_id": "012332", "plant": "P001",
 "valid_temperature": true, "known_unit": true, "valid_plant_code": true, ...}

docs.title: Available checks
docs.text:
All checks are imported from streamdaq.checks.

Check Parameters True when InRange name, column, low, high, inclusive_low=True, inclusive_high=False low <= value < high (bounds inclusive or exclusive as set) InSet name, column, allowed_values the value is in allowed_values Regex name, column, regex the value matches regex, starting at its beginning Length name, column, must_be the value's length (as text) satisfies must_be Value name, column, must_be, transformation=None the value, optionally transformed first, satisfies must_be InRowComparison name, columns (two column names), operator operator(first, second) holds, with operator one of "lt", "le", "eq", "ne", "gt", "ge"

For how to write must_be, see Assessments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from streamdaq.checks import InRowComparison, Length, Value

# Product codes must be between 4 and 8 characters long
Length(name="valid_code_length", column="product_code", must_be="[4, 8]")

# Humidity in percent, given as a fraction in the data
Value(name="valid_humidity", column="humidity", must_be="[0, 100]", transformation=lambda h: h * 100)

# A reading's start must come before its end
InRowComparison(name="start_before_end", columns=["start", "end"], operator="lt")

Regex matches from the start

Regex checks whether the pattern matches at the beginning of the value, like Python's re.match. To require the whole value to match, end the pattern with $, e.g. r"P\d{3}$".

Check names and column names

Check results are added next to the input columns. A check with the same name as an input column replaces that column in the results, so give checks names that differ from your columns.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Stream DaQ logs through Python's standard logging module, under the streamdaq logger. When you import Stream DaQ, it sets up logging with these defaults:

  • Stream DaQ's own messages at INFO level and above, printed to the terminal;
  • Pathway's messages at WARNING level and above;
  • Stream DaQ's messages are kept separate from your application's own logging.

docs.title: Changing the setup
docs.text:
Call configure_logging to change it:

import logging

from streamdaq.logging import configure_logging

configure_logging(level=logging.WARNING, pathway_level=None)
Setting Default Meaning level logging.INFO Minimum level for Stream DaQ's messages. pathway_level logging.WARNING Minimum level for Pathway's messages. None silences them. enable_console True Print Stream DaQ's messages to the terminal. log_format "[%(asctime)s] [%(levelname)s] [%(name)s]: %(message)s" Format of each line. date_format "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" Format of the time in each line.

docs.title: Sending logs elsewhere
docs.text:
Add handlers to the streamdaq logger, e.g. to write to a file instead of the terminal:

import logging

from streamdaq.logging import JsonFormatter, configure_logging

configure_logging(enable_console=False)

handler = logging.FileHandler("streamdaq.log")
handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())  # one JSON object per line
logging.getLogger("streamdaq").addHandler(handler)

For other destinations, implement a LogHook (with emit, flush and close) and attach it with LogHookHandler(hook).

docs.title: Measures
docs.text:
A measure is what a window check computes over each window. All measures are imported from streamdaq.measures, and the first argument is always the column to measure:

from streamdaq.measures import Count, InRangeFraction, Percentiles

Count("temperature")
InRangeFraction("temperature", low=-30, high=50, precision=2)
Percentiles("temperature", percentiles=[5, 50, 95])

Rounding with precision

Measures marked in the Prec. column accept precision=<digits> to round their result, e.g. Mean("temperature", precision=2).

Column types

Measures are grouped by the kind of column they apply to. Using a measure on a column of another kind, such as a numeric measure on a text column, is not allowed and is rejected.

docs.title: Any column
docs.text: Measure Parameters Prec. Returns Count Number of rows. Min, Max Smallest / largest value. Tuple All values, as a tuple. SortedTupleValue All values, sorted. SortedTupleTime time_column All values, ordered by time_column. Ndarray All values, as a NumPy array. WindowDuration window_end - window_start. Availability min_samples=1 True if the window has at least min_samples rows. Constancy How often the most common value occurs. MostFrequent The most common value(s), as a tuple (all ties included). MostFrequentApprox Approximate most common value(s), as a tuple of text values. DistinctCount Number of different values. DistinctFraction Different values ÷ rows. DistinctCountApprox Approximate number of different values (HyperLogLog). DistinctFractionApprox Approximate different values ÷ rows. UniqueCount Number of values that occur exactly once. UniqueFraction Values occurring once ÷ rows. UniqueOverDistinct Values occurring once ÷ different values. MissingCount disguised=[] Number of missing values: None, "", and any value in disguised (e.g. ["N/A", -1]). MissingFraction disguised=[] Missing values ÷ rows. DistinctPlaceholderCount placeholders How many of the given placeholder values appear. DistinctPlaceholderFraction placeholders That number ÷ rows. InSetCount allowed_values, only_most_frequent=False Number of values in allowed_values. InSetFraction allowed_values, only_most_frequent=False Values in allowed_values ÷ rows. Monotonic time_column, direction="asc", strict=True True if the values, ordered by time_column, only go up ("asc") or down ("desc"). Correlation other_column, method="pearson" Correlation with other_column: "pearson", "spearman", "kendall" or "cramer".

docs.title: Numeric columns
docs.text: Measure Parameters Prec. Returns Mean Average. Median Median. Sum Sum. Variance Population variance. StandardDeviation Population standard deviation. Percentiles percentiles=[25, 50, 75] {percentile: value}. For [18.0, 21.5, 24.0] the JSON output is {"25": 19.75, "50": 21.5, "75": 22.75}. AboveMeanCount Number of values above the mean. AboveMeanFraction Values above the mean ÷ rows. InRangeCount low, high, inclusive_low=True, inclusive_high=False, only_most_frequent=False Number of values in the range. InRangeFraction same as InRangeCount Values in the range ÷ rows. FrozenNumbers epsilon=0.0, min_samples=1 True if the window has at least min_samples values and they vary by at most epsilon: the signal looks "frozen". BestLineFitSlope time_column Slope of the best-fit line of the values over time_column: the trend. DeltasTuple time_column Differences between consecutive values, ordered by time_column. MinDelta, MaxDelta, MeanDelta, MedianDelta time_column Smallest / largest / mean / median of those differences. FirstDigitFreqs {digit: (count, share)} of first digits, e.g. to compare with Benford's law. MinIntegerPartLength, MaxIntegerPartLength, MeanIntegerPartLength, MedianIntegerPartLength Number of digits before the decimal point. MinFractionalPartLength, MaxFractionalPartLength, MeanFractionalPartLength, MedianFractionalPartLength Number of digits after the decimal point.

docs.title: Text columns
docs.text: Measure Parameters Prec. Returns MinLength, MaxLength Shortest / longest value length. MeanLength, MedianLength Mean / median value length. RegexCount regex Number of values matching regex from their start. RegexFraction regex Matching values ÷ rows.

docs.title: Counting only the most frequent values
docs.text:
InSetCount, InSetFraction, InRangeCount and InRangeFraction take only_most_frequent=True to look only at the window's most frequent value(s). The count then includes every occurrence of a most frequent value that conforms, and the fractions divide it by all rows in the window.

Window Measure Result [1, 1, 1, 2] InSetCount(..., allowed_values={1}, only_most_frequent=True) 3 [1, 1, 1, 2] InSetFraction(..., allowed_values={1}, only_most_frequent=True) 0.75 [1, 1, 2, 2, 3] InSetCount(..., allowed_values={1, 2}, only_most_frequent=True) 4 (tied values both count)

docs.title: Your own measures
docs.text: If no built-in measure fits, write your own with @measure. See Custom Code.

docs.title: REST API and CLI
docs.text: Stream DaQ can run as a service: you start a server, then create, inspect and remove monitoring tasks over HTTP, without writing Python.

docs.title: Starting the server
docs.text:
streamdaq serve

🪡  Initialized a streamdaq API session with name 'streamdaq_api_session'.
🌱 The streamdaq root directory is set to '/home/me/project/' (reusing existing root)
🦆 Attempting to start streamdaq API on http://127.0.0.1:8080.
ℹ️  Visit http://127.0.0.1:8080/docs for API Swagger UI.

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/docs for interactive API documentation, where you can also try every request.

Option Default Meaning -H, --host 127.0.0.1 Address to listen on. -P, --port 8080 Port to listen on. -R, --root ./ Folder for the server's stored state. Relative paths are resolved from the current folder. -C, --clear off Start from scratch: delete the stored tasks and watermarks in --root. -F, --files none A file or folder of custom code to load. -S, --session streamdaq_api_session A name for the session, shown at startup.

On startup, the server resumes the tasks that were running when it last stopped (unless --clear is given). Press Ctrl+C to stop it; running tasks are stopped too.

Use an absolute --root for services

Tasks are stored in --root. If you start the server from a different folder with a relative --root, it uses a different, empty store, and your earlier tasks seem to be gone. For services and containers, use an absolute path.

Check whether a server is running with:

streamdaq status            # same --host / --port options

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
All endpoints start with /api/v1.

Method Path What it does POST /bulk_create Create tasks, or update running ones. GET /tasks All stored tasks, by name. GET /tasks/{name} One task's configuration. DELETE /tasks/{name} Stop and remove a task. GET /session Server status: number of tasks and Stream DaQ version. GET /heartbeat {"status": "OK", "service": "streamdaq"} if the server is up. GET /config/options Everything you can use in a task: sources, sinks, windows, instant checks and measures, including custom ones.

docs.title: Creating and updating tasks
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/bulk_create takes a list of tasks. For each one:

  • if no task has that name yet, it's created and started;
  • if a task with that name exists, it's replaced by the new configuration while running. See Hot-swapping.
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/bulk_create \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @tasks.json
Response
{"message": "Successfully processed 1 task requests", "task_ids": ["readings"], "details": ["readings was created and started"]}

docs.title: Removing a task
docs.text: DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{name} stops the task and removes its configuration and watermarks. Its output files or topics are not touched.

docs.title: Task status
docs.text:
GET /tasks and GET /tasks/{name} include a status:

  • running: the task's process is running.
  • finished: the process has stopped, whether it completed normally or crashed.

docs.title: Task configuration
Task
docs.text: Field Required Meaning name yes Unique name of the task. input yes {"type": ..., "params": {...}}. See Inputs and Outputs. output yes {"type": ..., "params": {...}}. See Inputs and Outputs. instant_checks one of these two List of instant checks. window_checks_config one of these two Window checks and their window. wait_for_late no How long to wait for late data, in time-column units. include_streamdaq_metadata no Add _streamdaq_metadata to results (default true).

docs.title: Instant check
docs.text: Field Meaning name Name of the result column. check_class InRange, InSet, Regex, Length, Value or InRowComparison. params The check's parameters except name, e.g. {"column": "temperature", "low": -30, "high": 50}.

docs.title: Window checks
docs.text:
Field Required Meaning windowby_column yes The column holding when each event happened. window yes {"type": "tumbling" \| "sliding" \| "session", "params": {...}}, e.g. {"duration": 60} or {"hop": 10, "duration": 60}. checks yes List of {"name", "measure": {"type", "params"}, "must_be"}. must_be is optional. groupby_column no Separate windows per value of this column. See Grouping. include_window_bounds no Add window_start/window_end (default true).

Measure params are the measure's parameters, e.g. {"column": "temperature"}; see Measures.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Requests are checked before any task starts. Common errors:

  • an unknown type, check_class or measure, or invalid parameters for it;
  • a must_be that is neither a comparison or range nor a registered assessment;
  • "Input configuration is required." / "Output configuration is required.";
  • "At least one instant check or window check is required.".

docs.title: Tasks and Sessions
docs.text: A task describes one monitoring job: where the data comes from, which checks to apply, and where the results go. A session runs tasks.

docs.title: A minimal task
docs.text:
A task with one per-row check and one per-window check
import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.checks import InRange, WindowDataQualityCheck
from streamdaq.measures import Count
from streamdaq.sessions import Session
from streamdaq.tasks import Task


class Reading(pw.Schema):
    timestamp: int
    temperature: float


def read_stream() -> pw.Table:  # (1)!
    return pw.io.jsonlines.read("readings.jsonl", schema=Reading, mode="streaming")


task = Task(
    name="readings",
    input=read_stream,
    output=pw.io.jsonlines.write,  # (2)!
    output_kwargs={"filename": "quality.jsonl"},
    windowby_column="timestamp",
)
task.add_instant_checks(
    InRange(name="valid_temperature", column="temperature", low=-30, high=50),
)
task.add_window_checks(
    WindowDataQualityCheck("enough_readings", Count("temperature"), ">= 5"),
    window=pw.temporal.tumbling(duration=60),
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    Session(tasks=[task]).start()
  1. Any function that returns a Pathway table can be the input. See Inputs and Outputs.
  2. Any function that takes a pw.Table can be the output. The per-window results go to quality_window.jsonl, see Where results go.

docs.title: Task settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does name None The task's name. Required when the task is added to a session. input required A function returning a pw.Table, called as input(**input_kwargs). output required A function taking a pw.Table, called as output(table, **output_kwargs). input_kwargs / output_kwargs {} Keyword arguments passed to input / output. windowby_column None The column holding when each event happened. Needed for window checks. groupby_column None Gives each value of this column its own windows. See Window Checks. wait_for_late None How long to keep a window open for late events. See Window Checks. include_window_bounds True Adds window_start and window_end to every window result. include_streamdaq_metadata True Adds a _streamdaq_metadata column, e.g. {"task_name": "readings", "task_version": 1}.

Checks are added with:

  • task.add_instant_checks(*checks): checks applied to every row. See Instant Checks.
  • task.add_window_checks(*checks, window=...): checks applied to each window of rows. The window applies to all window checks of the task. See Window Checks.

Both return the task, so the calls can be chained.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
A task produces up to two result streams, both written to the task's output:

Results Contents Per-row (instant checks) every input column, plus one True/False column per instant check Per-window (window checks) window_start, window_end, the group (if any), one column per window check

The per-window results go to a separate destination; see Where results go.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A session runs tasks. Each task runs in its own process, so tasks don't slow each other down.

session = Session(tasks=[task_a, task_b])
session.start()
Setting Default What it does tasks [] The tasks to run. More can be added with session.add_tasks(...). root_path "./" Folder where the session keeps its state (.streamdaq_db/, .internals/). clear False Delete the stored state in root_path when the session starts. files_path None A file or folder of custom code to load in every task process.

Every task needs a unique name

Tasks are identified by their names, so Session and add_tasks reject a task without a name, or with a name already in the session.

docs.title: Starting and stopping
docs.text:
• session.start() starts every task that isn't running yet, and returns immediately.
  • session.gracefully_kill(timeout_seconds) stops every task: it asks each process to stop, and kills it if it hasn't stopped after timeout_seconds.

Running tasks from a Jupyter notebook needs one extra step; see Good to Know.

docs.title: Running tasks as a service
docs.text:
Instead of writing Python, you can run Stream DaQ as a server and send tasks to it as JSON:

streamdaq serve

See REST API and CLI. Tasks created this way are stored, can be changed while running, and are resumed after a restart; see Hot-swapping and Persistence.

docs.title: Window Checks
docs.text:
Window checks look at groups of rows over time. Stream DaQ cuts the stream into windows by event time, computes a measure over each window (a count, a mean, the number of distinct values...), and optionally assesses whether the result is good.

import pathway as pw

from streamdaq.checks import WindowDataQualityCheck
from streamdaq.measures import Count, DistinctCount, Mean

task = Task(name="readings", input=read_stream, output=..., windowby_column="timestamp")
task.add_window_checks(
    WindowDataQualityCheck("enough_readings", Count("temperature"), ">= 5"),
    WindowDataQualityCheck("mean_temperature", Mean("temperature")),
    WindowDataQualityCheck("few_units", DistinctCount("unit_id"), "<= 10"),
    window=pw.temporal.tumbling(duration=60),
)
One per-window result
{"window_start": 0, "window_end": 60, "enough_readings": true, "mean_temperature": 21.4, "few_units": true,
 "_streamdaq_metadata": {"task_name": "readings", "task_version": 1}, ...}

docs.title: Anatomy of a window check
docs.text:
WindowDataQualityCheck(name, measure, must_be=None)
Part Meaning name The name of the result column. measure What to compute over each window, e.g. Count("temperature"). See Measures. must_be Optional. What a good value is, e.g. ">= 5" or "(5, 15]". See Assessments.
  • Without must_be, the column holds the measured value ("mean_temperature": 21.4).
  • With must_be, the column holds only the result of the assessment ("enough_readings": true). The measured value itself is not output.

Seeing the value and the verdict

To get both, add two checks with the same measure, one with must_be and one without:

WindowDataQualityCheck("reading_count", Count("temperature")),
WindowDataQualityCheck("enough_readings", Count("temperature"), ">= 5"),

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Windows are given to add_window_checks with window=. All window checks of a task share the same window. The task's windowby_column tells Stream DaQ which column holds when each event happened; windows are based on that time, not on when rows arrive.

Window Created with Use it for Tumbling pw.temporal.tumbling(duration=60) Fixed, back-to-back windows: [0, 60), [60, 120), ... Sliding pw.temporal.sliding(hop=10, duration=60) Overlapping windows: a 60-unit window starting every 10 units. Each row belongs to several windows. Session pw.temporal.session(max_gap=30) Windows that follow bursts of activity: events less than max_gap apart go into the same window, and a gap longer than max_gap starts a new one. Windows can have any length.

Durations are in the same units as windowby_column: plain numbers for numeric time columns (e.g. milliseconds for EVB data), or datetime.timedelta for datetime columns.

When are window results reported?

Each window reports its results exactly once, as soon as the event time in the stream passes the end of the window (plus wait_for_late, see below).

docs.title: Window bounds
docs.text: By default every window result starts with window_start and window_end, so you know which period it describes. Turn them off with include_window_bounds=False on the task.

docs.title: Grouping
docs.text:
By default each window covers all rows. With groupby_column, every value of that column gets its own windows, and every result row says which group it belongs to:

task = Task(..., windowby_column="timestamp", groupby_column="unit_id")

{"window_start": 0, "window_end": 60, "unit_id": "012332", "enough_readings": true, ...}
{"window_start": 0, "window_end": 60, "unit_id": "012385", "enough_readings": false, ...}

To group by several columns, combine them into one column first; see Advanced Examples.

docs.title: Late data
docs.text:
Events don't always arrive in order. By default a window is closed as soon as event time reaches its end, and events for it that arrive later are not counted.

wait_for_late keeps each window open a little longer, in the units of windowby_column:

task = Task(..., windowby_column="timestamp", wait_for_late=5)

With wait_for_late=5, the window [0, 60) is reported once event time reaches 65, and events with timestamps in [0, 60) arriving before that are still counted.

wait_for_late Results Late events None (default) as soon as a window ends dropped once the window has ended higher later counted, if they arrive within the wait

See Real-time Monitoring for the trade-offs.
